partial_case.facts: The property is a 2-bedroom flat on the first (top) floor. The resident reported damp and mould from March 2024 to January 2025. The landlord inspected in May and December 2024 and recommended treating all affected rooms (kitchen, bathroom, bedroom and living room). It attended on 16 January 2025 to treat the bedroom and bathroom. The resident complained on 4 March 2025 that she had reported damp and mould for years, the landlord had failed to attend that day to complete works, the treatment was failing, and mould was returning in the living room. She said she was vulnerable and disabled with severe asthma. The landlord's stage 1 response on 25 March 2025 upheld the complaint because of delays, communication failures and a missed appointment on 4 March 2025. It apologised, offered £100 compensation, and said it would revisit to inspect the damp and mould and the gutters. The resident replied the same day, saying there were errors in the response and disputed some details and the compensation offer. On 22 April 2025, the resident asked to escalate the complaint, saying the landlord had visited that day and tried to blame her for the mould. The landlord's stage 2 response on 30 May 2025 upheld the complaint as there were outstanding repairs and a lack of communication. It offered a further £100 compensation. The resident has confirmed all works were completed in September 2025, which seem to have resolved the damp and mould. She has asked for an apology and her rent arrears to be cleared in place of compensation for loss of wages and damage to furniture, carpets and personal items.
partial_case.ground_truth_outcome: Maladministration found in landlord's handling of damp and mould and complaint handling. Orders made for apology, compensation of £700 total (£600 for damp and mould handling, £100 for complaint handling), reinspection in January 2026, recording vulnerabilities, and insurance claim information.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: There were unreasonable delays and communication failures in the landlord's handling of the damp and mould. It offered redress but this was insufficient considering the failures identified, and the impact on the resident.
The landlord delayed in escalating the resident's stage 2 complaint. She took time and trouble to get this escalated. It did not acknowledge its failures or offer any redress.
This was significantly over the landlord's 20 working day committed timescale for routine repairs, set out in its repairs policy.
There is no evidence the landlord reached any conclusions about the cause of the damp and mould at any of its 4 inspections in May and December 2024 or April 2025.
This was an unreasonable delay, and was particularly concerning given the potential links to the damp and mould and the resident's concerns about her health.

claimed_amounts.description: Resident asked for her £2,500 rent arrears to be cleared instead of compensation.

evidence: The landlord inspected the property in May and December 2024 and attended on 16 January 2025 to treat the bedroom and bathroom.

The Ombudsman referred to the landlord’s repairs policy, complaints policy, the resident’s tenancy agreement, operative notes, inspection records, and the landlord’s evidence submission about recorded vulnerabilities.
partial_case.facts: The case concerns London Borough of Hounslow, a local authority landlord, and a secure tenancy in a 2-bedroom first-floor/top-floor flat. The complaint was about the landlord’s handling of damp and mould, and the Ombudsman also investigated complaint handling. Between March 2024 and January 2025, the resident reported damp and mould; the landlord inspected in May and December 2024, recommended treating affected rooms, and attended on 16 January 2025 to treat the bedroom and bathroom. On 4 March 2025, the resident complained that she had reported damp and mould for years, that the landlord had failed to attend that day to complete works, that treatment was failing and mould was returning in the living room, and that she was vulnerable and disabled with severe asthma. On 25 March 2025, the landlord’s stage 1 response apologised, offered £100 compensation, and said it would revisit to inspect the damp and mould and gutters; the resident disputed some details and the compensation offer. On 22 April 2025, the resident asked to escalate the complaint and said the landlord had visited that day and tried to blame her for the mould. On 30 May 2025, the landlord’s stage 2 response offered a further £100 compensation. The resident confirmed all works were completed in September 2025 and appeared to have resolved the damp and mould; she asked for an apology and for rent arrears to be cleared instead of compensation for loss of wages and damage to furniture, carpets and personal items.

orders: £700 compensation total, made up of £600 for damp and mould and £100 for complaint handling
write to the resident about making an insurance claim for damaged items

key_reasoning_quotes.text: There were unreasonable delays and communication failures in the landlord’s handling of the damp and mould. It offered redress but this was insufficient considering the failures identified, and the impact on the resident.
The landlord delayed in escalating the resident’s stage 2 complaint. She took time and trouble to get this escalated. It did not acknowledge its failures or offer any redress.
The landlord must address damp and mould in line with section 9A of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.
It is vital that landlords seek to identify the underlying cause of damp and mould and resolve this, as well as treating the problem.
The landlord did not consistently do that. It was often only in response to the resident chasing that action was taken or updates provided.
Overall, there was maladministration in the landlord’s complaint handling.
